books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Oregon and Maine boundary settlements: Britain and the United States had shared the Oregon Country since 1818 under “joint occupation.” By the 1840s American settlers were pouring in along the Oregon Trail, and the cry “Fifty-four forty or fight” demanded the whole territory to the line of 54°40′ latitude. In 1846 President Polk, already at war with Mexico, compromised with Britain at the 49th parallel, the present border. Four years earlier, the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842 had settled a different border fight: it split the disputed land along the Maine–New Brunswick border after the bloodless “Aroostook War” of 1838–1839, and it closed the Caroline incident of 1837, in which British forces had burned an American ship, with both sides admitting wrongdoing.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Webster-Ashburton Treaty (1842) and the Oregon boundary settlement (1846). Paraphrased, not quoted; public domain sources.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Polk accepted the 49th parallel for Oregon rather than fighting for 54°40′ mainly because

options.text: Britain had already agreed to give up all of Oregon without a fight
options.misconception: Britain refused; the 49th parallel was a compromise.

options.text: the United States was at war with Mexico and could not fight Britain too
American settlers had refused to move to Oregon in large numbers
options.misconception: Settlers were pouring in; that was the pressure for the whole territory.

options.text: Congress had voted to abandon the Oregon Country entirely
options.misconception: Congress never voted to abandon it.

rationales.A: Britain held firm on keeping part of Oregon. The 49th parallel was a compromise, not a British surrender.
rationales.B: Polk's slogan promised the whole territory, but by 1846 the United States was at war with Mexico. Fighting Britain at the same time would have meant two wars at once, so he settled.
rationales.C: The passage says settlers were pouring in along the Oregon Trail. Their arrival pushed Polk to claim the land, not to give it up.
rationales.D: No such vote took place. The decision was Polk's, made because a second war was more than the country could fight.
rationales.general:
1. Read the slogan. “Fifty-four forty or fight” demanded the whole Oregon Country.
2. Read the timing. Polk compromised in 1846, the same year the war with Mexico began.
3. Put it together. A president already fighting one war cannot start a second one over a border.
Background: The 49th parallel became the present border between the western United States and Canada.
Remember: when a bold slogan ends in compromise, ask what other fight was already under way.
